name: librsync
desc: Library that implements the rsync remote-delta algorithm
why: Implements rsync's rolling-checksum delta algorithm as a library, a clever idea hidden under a lot of everyday plumbing.

brief.what_it_is: librsync is a C library for calculating and applying network deltas, the rsync remote-delta algorithm packaged as an API for other programs. To compute a delta you need only a signature (per-block checksums) of the old file plus the new file, not both files together. The tree also builds an rdiff command-line tool that exposes the key operations: generating a file signature, generating a delta from a signature to a new file, and applying the delta to rebuild the new file from the old one. It works on byte streams only.
brief.why_it_exists: It is meant for building other programs that transfer files as efficiently as rsync, such as backup tools, binary patch distribution, or directory sync to a server or between peers. It was originally written for the rproxy experiment in delta-compression for HTTP. The README says Dropbox, rdiff-backup and Duplicity use it.
brief.how_it_works: The receiver computes a signature: a set of checksums over each block of one file. The sender then scans the other file, and blocks at any position whose checksum matches are likely identical, while the remaining bytes are the difference. The README says this lets differences be transferred without both files being on the same system. It uses BLAKE2 for hashing, which the README says is included in the tree.

commands_seen.context: Named in the README as the command-line tool that exposes librsync's signature, delta, and patch operations. The README gives no concrete invocation, and I saw no example command lines.

brief.install_notes: Nothing beyond the package manager was described on the homepage. The README's Installing section is only linked, not reproduced, so I could not confirm build dependencies or steps. No accounts, runtimes, or first-run configuration were mentioned.
brief.standout: The rsync algorithm needs only checksums of one file, not the file itself, so the two sides never have to share a filesystem. The project also makes the point that it is a library: it deliberately leaves out the rsync wire protocol, SSH, and file metadata, so it fits into other programs rather than replacing rsync.
brief.status: Unknown, leaning quiet. The page shows version 2.3.4 and says the documentation was generated on Sun Feb 19 2023. I did not see a last-commit date or release history, so I cannot say more than that.
brief.caveats: It does not talk to an rsync server; you have to shell out to rsync for that. It does not handle filenames, permissions, or directories, and it has no network code of its own. Licensing is LGPL v2.1: you can link it dynamically into non-GPL programs, but you must redistribute librsync source with any modifications. The BLAKE2 code in the tree is CC0.
quotes: librsync is a library for calculating and applying network deltas, with an interface designed to ease integration into diverse network applications.
The rsync algorithm is different from most differencing algorithms because it does not require the presence of the two files to calculate the delta.
librsync does not implement the rsync wire protocol. If you want to talk to an rsync server to transfer files you'll need to shell out to rsync.
fetch_log: https://librsync.github.io/ — fetched OK; returned the rendered README (version 2.3.4). The README's Downloads, Installing, rdiff command and NEWS sections are linked but their contents were not included, so I did not follow them.

judge.reason: Its rolling-checksum delta algorithm can reconstruct a changed file using only the old file’s signature, making a subtle, widely useful idea easy to explore with rdiff.

entry.title: librsync
entry.tldr: The rsync delta algorithm as a C library, plus rdiff, a tool that makes a patch from a tiny checksum file instead of the old file itself.
entry.deeper_look:
librsync packages the core trick of rsync as an API that other programs can call. The `rdiff` tool that comes with it exposes three operations: make a signature of a file, make a delta from that signature and a newer file, and apply the delta to the old file to rebuild the new one.

The unusual part is the first step. The signature is a set of checksums, one per block of the old file. To compute a delta, the other side needs only that signature and the new file. In the README's words, "The rsync algorithm is different from most differencing algorithms because it does not require the presence of the two files to calculate the delta." The two machines never need to see each other's whole file.

The sender scans the new file and looks for blocks whose checksums match the signature, at any byte offset. Matches are likely identical and become references to the old file. The leftover bytes are the difference. That idea sits under backup tools and binary patch distribution. The README says Dropbox, rdiff-backup and Duplicity use it. It began as part of rproxy, an experiment in delta compression for HTTP.

The scope is deliberately narrow. It works on byte streams only, with no filenames, permissions, directories, network code or rsync wire protocol. That leaves the algorithm easy to see by itself.

try_this.what_happens: Lists the tool's operations and options, including the signature, delta and patch steps.

entry.whats_unique: It is the rsync algorithm on its own, as a reusable library with no wire protocol, SSH or file metadata. That makes it a way to study the delta idea and to build your own sync or backup tool.
entry.caveats: It does not talk to an rsync server, and it handles only byte streams, not filenames, permissions or directories; the homepage shows version 2.3.4 with docs generated in February 2023.
